analysis.one_liner: Extends Medicaid and CHIP coverage for low-income mothers from 60 days to a full year after pregnancy, and adds dental coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 19 House Democrats and no Republicans, was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on July 21, 2026, and has had no hearings, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The MOMMIES Act would extend Medicaid and CHIP coverage for pregnant and postpartum people from 60 days after pregnancy to a full year, and require that coverage to include dental care. It would create a five-year grant program helping states build 'maternity care homes' that coordinate prenatal care, doulas, mental health support, and social services for Medicaid patients. It would also require Medicaid to pay primary care and maternity providers at Medicare-level rates, and direct federal agencies to report on coverage gaps, doula access, and telehealth for maternity care.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income pregnant and postpartum people enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP, the programs that pay for roughly four in ten births in the United States. Today they can lose coverage 60 days after pregnancy ends, often just as postpartum health risks like depression, bleeding, and heart problems peak. The bill would guarantee a full year of coverage with dental care included, plus better access to doulas, community health workers, and coordinated maternity care. Community health centers, birth centers, and doulas would also gain new funding and payment rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income mothers on Medicaid and CHIP

how_it_helps.text: Extends Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for pregnant and postpartum people from a 60-day postpartum window to one full year, with states free to go longer, and requires full benefits for that period regardless of which eligibility basis the person qualified under [S2][S3]
Adds oral health services — preventive, diagnostic, periodontal, and restorative dental care — as a required benefit for pregnant and postpartum people in Medicaid and CHIP [S2][S3]

Creates a five-year demonstration project providing grants to at least 10 states to implement maternity care homes that coordinate prenatal and postpartum care, doulas, community health workers, mental health treatment, and social services like housing and transportation, with priority for states with the worst maternal health disparities [S2][S3]

Requires Medicaid to pay primary care and maternity providers — including OB-GYNs, midwives, and clinics — at no less than Medicare payment rates, with up to a 25 percent boost in rural and underserved areas, to draw more providers into Medicaid maternity care [S3]

Directs MACPAC to report on doula coverage in state Medicaid programs and CMS to issue guidance on expanding doula access at pay levels that let doulas earn a living wage, and directs the GAO to report on Medicaid coverage gaps and on telehealth for maternity care [S2][S3]

Bars states from tightening eligibility or cutting benefits for pregnant Medicaid and CHIP enrollees during the phase-in period, and the federal government would pick up 100 percent of the cost of the newly required coverage [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of the extended coverage (the bill promises 100 percent federal matching funds for the new requirements), the grant program (funded by unspecified 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2034), and the higher Medicaid provider payment rates. States give up flexibility to restrict eligibility or trim benefits for pregnant enrollees during the maintenance-of-effort window, though the 100 percent match limits their direct new costs. Medicaid managed care insurers would have to pay primary care providers at the higher required rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; states lose some flexibility

drawbacks.text: The bill is an open-ended expansion of entitlements and grants: the maternity care home program is authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' for eight fiscal years, and the one-year postpartum entitlement and 100 percent federal match would add substantial, ongoing federal Medicaid spending [S3]

Raising Medicaid primary care payments to Medicare rates is a lasting cost increase for the Medicaid program, and states would bear the cost of the rate floor for services not covered by the 100 percent match for the new postpartum requirements [S3]

The maternity care home model is a demonstration project — the bill itself cannot guarantee that coordinating care through grants to community entities will lower maternal deaths or spending, which is why it requires an outside evaluator and reports before any wider adoption [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — a full year of postpartum Medicaid coverage instead of 60 days — targets a well-documented gap in a program that pays for a large share of US births, and many states have already adopted the one-year extension on their own, which suggests the model is workable. The costs are real but ordinary for health entitlements: more federal Medicaid spending, an uncapped grant program, and higher provider payment rates. The bill is transparent about what is unproven, gating the maternity care home model behind evaluation. The main honest objection is fiscal scale and design, not that the benefits are speculative — the year of coverage is a concrete, immediate benefit to a defined group.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, markup, or floor vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the MOMMIES Act on July 21, 2026, with 18 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3][S4]
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearings, no markup, no vote — since that referral [S2][S5]
All 19 sponsors are House Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored the bill in a chamber where Republicans hold 223 of 441 seats [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet from the outcome itself. The bill's fate so far has been decided by inaction in committee, which leaves the status quo in place: the existing 60-day postpartum coverage window, voluntary state-by-state extensions, and current Medicaid payment rates for maternity providers. Medicaid programs and payers avoid new spending requirements, and the low-income mothers the bill would cover are no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one — the bill sits untouched in committee

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 21, 2026; the committee has taken no further action — no hearing or markup has been scheduled since [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic — 19 House Democrats including the sponsor, with zero Republican cosponsors in a House where Republicans hold a narrow 223-218 majority [S4].

industries.note: Extended postpartum eligibility means more enrolled member-months and more revenue flowing through Medicaid managed care contracts, so insurers' interest runs alongside the coverage expansion. The bill does impose one new cost on them: contracts must pay primary care providers at the required minimum rates.

industries.industry: Obstetric, primary care, and clinic providers
industries.note: Medicaid currently pays providers far less than Medicare; the bill sets a Medicare-rate floor for primary care and maternity providers, with up to 25 percent more in rural and underserved areas. Better pay is meant to pull more clinicians into caring for Medicaid patients.

industries.industry: Doulas, community health workers, and birth centers
industries.note: The bill funds doula and community-based maternity workforces through the demonstration grants and directs CMS to push states toward doula reimbursement at living-wage levels, opening a paid pathway for workers who are largely outside the current payment system.

States would face a maintenance-of-effort bar on tightening eligibility or cutting benefits for pregnant enrollees, plus the cost of the provider payment floor outside the 100 percent match. The 100 percent federal match on the new coverage requirements limits their direct financial exposure.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a narrow House majority and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is unlikely to receive a committee markup or floor vote this Congress. Comparable Medicaid maternal-health expansion bills introduced by minority-party members in past Congresses have typically died in committee without a hearing.
